candidates.title: Nebius tests the neocloud playbook with $40 billion in planned spending
candidates.snippet: Nebius plans to fund its $40 billion AI infrastructure expansion through customer prepayments and loans, even as delays at a Microsoft data center raise questions about its financing model.
candidates.text:
In its third-quarter earnings call Thursday, the neocloud company Nebius laid out $40 billion in planned spending for 2027, far more than Wall Street had expected. It’s an ambitious plan, but it rests on a string of planned projects that are already starting to show cracks.
Nebius plans to fund the buildout by relying on customer pre-payments and loans backed by customer contracts — essentially using the future value of its data centers to finance their construction. But that can be a risky strategy if those projects get bogged down by delays or cancellations.
“Building at this scale is hard, and delays are part of our industry right now,” CEO Arkady Volozh said during Thursday’s earnings call. “We are not immune.”
The earnings announcement comes on the heels of reports that Microsoft is cooling on neocloud deals that aren’t delivering on time. That’s a problem for companies like Nebius, whose financing strategy is becoming more dependent on repayments. Because if it can’t get to capacity on time, it will keep piling on costs while revenues slip.
One of Nebius’ largest customers is Microsoft, which is paying for AI computing capacity at a Vineland, New Jersey, data center that is now months behind schedule. Nebius’ contract with Microsoft is worth up to $19.4 billion, but it’s already letting deadlines slip. Only just over half of the Microsoft capacity is now planned for delivery by the end of the year, with the rest coming in Q2 2027.
The delay is because DataOne, the third-party operator of the site, “decided to wind down the temporary generation faster than it was expected,” according to Andrey Korolenko, chief product and infrastructure officer, as the site switches over to Bloom Energy fuel cells.
Still, that transition wasn’t entirely by choice. In August , the investigative site Floodlight identified at least 45 natural gas generators in operation at the DataOne site, even though it had not received any permits for operating gas generators. New Jersey regulators fined the DataOne facility $1.1 million in response, finding that the use of the generators violated federal law.
DataOne is also facing a noise-complaint lawsuit from nearby residents over a constant humming noise allegedly emitted by the data center.
According to Nebius’ summary of its Microsoft contract, Microsoft can terminate affected service after a grace period if dates are missed and no alternative capacity is offered. The tranches were originally meant to be deployed in 2025 and 2026, so a Q2 2027 delivery date falls well beyond that window. The contract also includes financial penalties for late delivery.
Nebius said that Microsoft “has been part of the planning process.” Nebius did not say whether Microsoft has agreed to the new dates, but Microsoft has not publicly canceled anything.
TechCrunch has reached out to Nebius, Microsoft, and DataOne for comment.
On the call, Marc Boroditsky, Nebius’s chief revenue officer, said the company’s deals with Microsoft and Meta both came with significant prepayment, which arrived long before delivery. But Bloomberg reported last week that Microsoft is tightening oversight on projects run by third parties, including Nebius, IREN, and Nscale, and debating whether it’s worth signing new agreements. Microsoft also sent employees to the site in New Jersey, per Bloomberg.
In its own quarterly earnings report, Microsoft noted that its capex spend was lower than expected due to third-party delays. The company is clearly not above pulling back from planned agreements where its partner doesn’t meet its share of the bargain. Bloomberg also reported that Microsoft won’t use an option to more than double its Nscale agreement for a Texas data center and recently stopped being an anchor customer for Nscale’s planned Essex site after power delays.
Nebius says the delays it faces are coming from sites it doesn’t control, with the data centers it is building itself coming online on time or ahead of schedule. Those, Nebius says, will supply most of its new capacity from 2027. New deals signed in Q3 came with prepayments that more than cover the cost of building capacity behind them, says Boroditsky. Nebius ended the quarter with $7.4 billion in cash.
Total prepayments plus asset-backed financing of investment-grade contracts are expected to cover up to 85% of the $40 to $45 billion 2027 capex spend. CFO Maria Del Dado Alonso Sanchez named Microsoft and Meta as contracts that can be financed this way. Boroditsky also said Nebius could “tap prepayments to shore up any additional cash requirements.”
Nebius forecast 2027 revenue of $12 to $13 billion, and said it expects to break even on a pre-tax basis by the fourth quarter.
Nebius reported third-quarter revenue of $981 million, up 571% from a year earlier. Roughly a third of that was a one-time payment tied to a new partnership model. Nebius cut its 2026 revenue forecast by $200 million to $3 billion, citing delays to third-party sites like New Jersey. Shares ended the day down 17%.

candidates.title: Hugging Face CEO vows to keep fighting for open source AI after Jensen Huang’s exit
candidates.snippet: Hugging Face's CEO pledged to keep fighting for open source AI after Huang's exit, raising questions about Nvidia's $12.9 billion acquisition.
candidates.text:
Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue briefly commented on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s departure on Thursday, calling it a “really sad day.” Nvidia had announced its plan to acquire the platform for open source AI models in September for $12.9 billion, making it the second-largest acquisition in the company’s history, just behind that of chipmaker Groq’s assets for $20 billion in December 2025.
“This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened. It’s a really sad day! But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go!,” Delangue wrote on X.
This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened. It’s a really sad day!
But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go! — clem 🤗 (@ClementDelangue) November 12, 2026
The post is interesting as it implies that Huang’s departure is potentially worrying to open source advocates, and he’s attempting to offer reassurance.
As Nvidia’s CEO, Huang was known as a strong advocate for open source AI and open-weight models, which is why there could be concerns about how a company that’s no longer under his leadership will now approach this space.
After Nvidia announced its plans to acquire Hugging Face, the U.S. Department of Justice began making inquiries about how the deal would impact competition in the AI market, Reuters reported in October . While Nvidia pledged that the platform would preserve open support, it would also allow the company to control a major distribution channel for AI models.
The Hugging Face deal is still scheduled to close in the first half of 2027. Requests for further comment on the deal status and whether Hugging Face has spoken yet with Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress were not returned.
Huang’s advocacy for open source and open-weight AI has long extended beyond Hugging Face. In July, the CEO published an AI policy letter as his first-ever post on the social network X . The letter, which was signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, Hugging Face, IBM, Palantir, and others, urged the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models. It said models that “anyone can download, inspect, modify, and run on their own infrastructure” are an important part of the AI ecosystem because they make AI “more accessible, adaptable, and widely available.”
Huang also wrote that open-weight models expand access to the AI economy, strengthen competition, and give customers greater control, as they know they won’t become locked into a single provider. “Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty,” his post on X stated.
For my first post, I’m sharing a letter @NVIDIA signed on why open models matter.
AI will transform every industry, power every company, and be built by every country.
Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty.… pic.twitter.com/t02bi51N4C — Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) July 24, 2026
In August, Nvidia also announced a $6 billion deal with the coding startup Poolside to help build out an open AI ecosystem in the U.S. to help the country compete against Chinese companies like DeepSeek and Kimi K3, The Wall Street Journal reported at the time. Last month, Nvidia expanded its Nemotron family of open-weight models with a large 120-billion-parameter model for agents used by the enterprise as well as with two new lightweight Bolt models that run on PCs.
Earlier this year, Huang promoted open source AI during his January keynote address at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas, noting that open source models have “really revolutionized artificial intelligence.”

UK-Backed AI Chip Startup Fractile Reaches $7B Valuation in $720M Series C
By James Dargan · 13 November 2026 · 1 min read
Fractile, a London- and Bristol-based AI chip startup, has been valued at $7 billion after securing $720 million in a Series C round that included backing from the British government, making it one of the UK’s most valuable technology startups.
The round was led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed and Redpoint, with participation from Google’s venture arm CapitalG, BlackRock, DST Global, Elad Gil, Balderton, SV Angel, Britain’s Sovereign AI fund and the British Business Bank.
Fractile is developing chips designed to improve AI inference, the process by which AI models generate responses, and says its technology delivers faster performance while reducing energy use and costs. The company plans to release its first commercial chip next year.
The deal signals confidence in Britain’s push to build domestic AI infrastructure rather than relying solely on overseas computing power, and reflects growing investor interest in AI hardware, a market dominated by Nvidia and a small group of Asian manufacturers.
AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said Britain has too often produced world-leading scientific ideas only to see the resulting technology, industry and wealth built elsewhere, and that the government is determined to change that. While the UK is home to chip designer Arm, its semiconductor manufacturing industry remains small compared with the US and Asia.

Norwest: $4 Billion Fund Expands Global Multi-Stage Investment Strategy
By Amit Chowdhry
Yesterday at 11:42 AM
Norwest: $4 Billion Fund Expands Global Multi-Stage Investment Strategy
Norwest has closed Norwest 18, a $4 billion global investment fund that will back venture and growth equity opportunities across technology, healthcare, and consumer markets. The vehicle is the largest fund in the firm’s 65-year history and increases its total capital under management to $18 billion.
Norwest will deploy the new fund across the United States, India, and Israel, continuing a strategy that spans early-stage venture investments through later-stage growth equity. The firm said this flexible approach allows it to begin working with companies at different stages and continue supporting them as their capital requirements and operating priorities evolve.
Since launching Norwest 17 in April 2024, the firm has completed more than 87 investments and worked with over 30 portfolio companies on liquidity events. Initial public offerings during that period included Amagi Media Labs, BillionToOne, MBX Biosciences, Omada Health, and Swiggy.
Strategic acquisitions involving Norwest-backed businesses included EQT’s acquisition of Avetta, Luminate Capital Partners’ purchase of AbsenceSoft, Gilead Sciences’ acquisition of Ouro Medicines, Salesforce’s purchase of Qualified, Pinterest’s acquisition of tvScientific, and ServiceNow’s purchase of Veza.
Norwest 18 will maintain the firm’s primary sector focus while increasing its exposure to emerging categories. Areas of interest include next-generation financial infrastructure, physical and voice AI, agentic cybersecurity, technology-enabled industrial and aerospace businesses, and healthcare AI.
Recent financial infrastructure investments include Beltic, Rain, and Stablecore. Norwest has also backed Coval, Generalist AI, and LlamaIndex in intelligent AI systems; Above Security, ORION Security, Red Access, and Zenity in cybersecurity; and East Range Group, Padmini VNA, JJG Aerospace, and Raghu Vamsi Aerospace Group in industrial and aerospace markets.
Healthcare investments include Infinx, Matchpoint Therapeutics, Rezo Therapeutics, Tokaido Health, and Vitalize Care. These businesses are applying AI to drug discovery, clinical and administrative workflows, healthcare access, and care-team productivity.
Beyond financing, Norwest provides portfolio companies with operating support and strategic guidance. The firm has doubled the size of its Senior Advisor Network, added operating executives, and launched the Norwest Operator Collective and Norwest Kinetic. These resources are intended to help management teams address technology, go-to-market, talent, and organizational challenges.
Since its founding in 1961, Norwest has invested in more than 750 companies and currently works with over 275 venture and growth equity portfolio companies. Its offices are in Menlo Park, San Francisco, Mumbai, and Tel Aviv.
KEY QUOTES
“Building and scaling a company has never been a linear journey, and today that journey is becoming more complex. Companies are staying private longer, scaling across markets, and navigating critical decisions around technology, talent, and growth. Capital is only one part of what they need. Our role is to be a long-term partner and bring the experience, networks, and resources that can help leadership teams make those decisions with confidence.”
Jeff Crowe, Senior Managing Partner at Norwest
“Markets and technology change, but what has remained consistent at Norwest is our ability to identify strong businesses, invest patiently, and stay closely aligned with the founders, CEOs, and leadership teams we partner with. Our multi-stage strategy allows us to meet companies where they are and continue supporting them as they grow. Norwest 18 gives us even greater flexibility to do that across sectors, stages, and geographies.”
Jon Kossow, Managing Partner at Norwest

Pfizer: Up To $1.5 Billion Funding Agreement With Blackstone Life Sciences To Advance Monthly GLP-1 Obesity Drug
By Amit Chowdhry
Yesterday at 2:21 PM
Pfizer: Up To $1.5 Billion Funding Agreement With Blackstone Life Sciences To Advance Monthly GLP-1 Obesity Drug
Pfizer and Blackstone Life Sciences have entered into a strategic funding agreement under which funds managed by Blackstone will provide up to $1.5 billion through 2028 to support the clinical development of berobenatide, Pfizer’s investigational monthly GLP-1 receptor agonist for chronic weight management and obesity-related conditions.
The agreement will help Pfizer advance its obesity drug development program while maintaining financial flexibility to invest in other therapeutic areas. In exchange for its funding commitment, Blackstone will become eligible for milestone-based payments tied to U.S. regulatory approval and commercial performance.
Berobenatide is being developed as a potential first-in-class monthly injectable GLP-1 receptor agonist peptide. Pfizer is evaluating the treatment for chronic weight management and obesity-related conditions, including knee osteoarthritis and obstructive sleep apnea.
The transaction represents a significant investment in Pfizer’s cardiometabolic pipeline as the pharmaceutical company advances a broad portfolio of investigational obesity therapies.
How The $1.5 Billion Funding Agreement Works
Under the agreement, Blackstone-managed funds will cover up to $1.5 billion in development expenses associated with berobenatide through 2028.
In return, Blackstone will be eligible to receive payments if the drug achieves specified regulatory and commercial milestones.
These payments are contingent on U.S. regulatory approval of monthly injectable berobenatide monotherapy for chronic weight management and the achievement of certain sales targets.
Any milestone payments earned by Blackstone would be distributed over multiple years.
The structure allows Pfizer to obtain external funding for a major clinical development program without selling ownership or commercial rights to the investigational medicine.
Pfizer will retain full operational control and decision-making authority over berobenatide, including its clinical development strategy.
The agreement also does not provide Blackstone with an ownership interest in the drug.
Funds managed by Blackstone’s perpetual private equity strategy, BXPE, will participate alongside funds managed by Blackstone Life Sciences.
The arrangement illustrates an alternative approach to financing pharmaceutical research, in which investment firms provide capital to support clinical development in exchange for payments linked to future milestones.
For Pfizer, the agreement provides an opportunity to share development costs while retaining control over a potentially important pipeline asset.
Berobenatide Targets Monthly GLP-1 Treatment
Berobenatide is an investigational GLP-1 receptor agonist peptide being studied for chronic weight management and related medical conditions.
GLP-1 receptor agonists act on biological pathways involved in appetite regulation, blood glucose control, and other metabolic processes.
Existing treatments in this drug class have established a significant market for obesity and metabolic disease therapies.
Pfizer is developing berobenatide as a potential monthly injectable treatment, which could offer a different administration schedule from therapies requiring more frequent dosing.
The company is pursuing an extensive clinical development program to evaluate the drug’s safety and effectiveness.
Pfizer plans to advance more than 20 clinical trials involving obesity and associated medical conditions during 2026.
These include 10 ongoing and planned Phase 3 trials for berobenatide.
The studies are intended to evaluate the treatment across chronic weight management and obesity-related conditions.
Pfizer is also investigating berobenatide in combination with other investigational therapies.
The company is studying combinations involving nutrient-stimulated hormone peptides, including amylin analogs.
These approaches are part of Pfizer’s broader strategy to develop treatments that act on multiple biological pathways associated with weight regulation and metabolic health.
Berobenatide remains investigational, and its safety, effectiveness, and potential approval have not yet been established by regulators.
Expanding Pfizer’s Cardiometabolic Pipeline
Pfizer is positioning berobenatide as a central component of its cardiometabolic research and development portfolio.
The company is evaluating the therapy both as a standalone treatment and in combination with other investigational medicines.
Its development strategy extends beyond weight loss to conditions associated with obesity.
Knee osteoarthritis and obstructive sleep apnea are among the conditions included in the clinical research program.
Obesity can contribute to a range of medical complications, creating opportunities for therapies that improve weight management and potentially address related health outcomes.
Pfizer’s clinical program is intended to generate evidence about berobenatide’s potential across different patient populations and treatment settings.
The agreement with Blackstone provides additional resources to support this work through 2028.
Pfizer said the funding arrangement will also allow it to maintain capacity for investment across its broader pharmaceutical pipeline.
By supplementing internal research spending with external capital, the company aims to pursue multiple development priorities simultaneously.

By Amit Chowdhry
Nov 12, 2026
Rowan Digital Infrastructure: $1.5 Billion In New Financing To Accelerate 5.5 GW Hyperscale Data Center Pipeline
Rowan Digital Infrastructure, a Denver-based developer of hyperscale data center campuses, has secured more than $1.5 billion in new corporate financing capacity to accelerate development of its 5.5-gigawatt project pipeline across the United States. The financing includes a $600 million expansion of its holding company term loan led by Apterra Infrastructure Capital, along with a new $590 million revolving credit facility and a $355 million letter of credit facility led by Citibank.
The transactions provide Rowan with additional financing flexibility to secure land, obtain power commitments, purchase equipment, and advance early-stage development activities across its portfolio of hyperscale data center projects.
With the latest transactions, Rowan has secured more than $8 billion in financing from over 40 lenders during the past 18 months.
The company’s development pipeline includes multiple large-scale data center campuses designed to support major technology companies and hyperscale computing operators.
Rowan has already contracted more than 1.2 gigawatts of capacity with major technology customers.
The additional corporate financing is intended to help the company accelerate the development of new facilities while maintaining access to capital across multiple projects.
$600 Million Term Loan Expansion
Rowan expanded its existing holding company credit facility by $600 million, increasing the total facility size to $900 million.
The original $300 million facility was established in September 2025 to support early-stage development activities.
Apterra Infrastructure Capital served as lead arranger for the expanded financing.
The additional term loan capacity provides Rowan with resources to support project development before individual campuses reach the construction financing stage.
These activities can include land acquisition, infrastructure planning, engineering, permitting, and coordination with electricity providers.
Early-stage financing is particularly important in hyperscale data center development because projects can require significant capital commitments before construction begins.
Rowan’s expanded corporate facility allows the company to pursue additional opportunities while progressing existing projects through development.
New $945 Million Credit Facilities Led By Citibank
In addition to the term loan expansion, Rowan established two new corporate credit facilities totaling $945 million.
The financing consists of a $590 million revolving credit facility and a $355 million letter of credit facility.
Citibank served as lead left arranger and administrative agent for both facilities.
The revolving credit arrangement provides Rowan with access to liquidity that can be borrowed, repaid, and borrowed again as its project pipeline develops.
This structure is intended to reduce the need for the company to obtain separate financing for every new development site.
The letter of credit facility provides financial support for obligations associated with project development.
These can include utility interconnection deposits, equipment vendor commitments, and other collateral requirements.
Letters of credit can help developers satisfy certain financial obligations without immediately posting equivalent amounts of cash.
Both facilities include provisions allowing for potential future expansion.
Subject to applicable conditions, Rowan may increase the revolving credit facility to as much as $2 billion and the letter of credit facility to as much as $1 billion.
These potential increases are not part of the initially committed $945 million.
The lender syndicate includes Citibank, Mizuho Bank, MUFG Bank, Goldman Sachs Bank USA, Societe Generale, Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation, and Huntington National Bank.
Several participating banks have previously supported Rowan’s project-level financing transactions.
Supporting A 5.5 GW Data Center Development Pipeline
Rowan is developing a portfolio of hyperscale data center campuses across multiple U.S. markets.
Its pipeline totals approximately 5.5 gigawatts of planned capacity, with more than 1.2 gigawatts already contracted.
The company specializes in build-to-suit infrastructure designed to support hyperscale operators requiring substantial computing capacity.
These facilities typically require extensive electrical infrastructure, specialized cooling systems, and significant investment in equipment and construction.
Access to electricity and the ability to deliver operational capacity quickly have become increasingly important factors in data center development.
Rowan’s business model emphasizes securing strategic locations and coordinating infrastructure development to meet customer requirements.
The new financing will help support these activities across the company’s growing portfolio.
Rowan is actively developing campuses ranging from approximately 300 megawatts to more than one gigawatt in capacity.
The company’s broader strategy is supported by investment partnerships with Quinbrook and Blackstone.
More Than $8 Billion In Recent Financing Activity
The latest corporate financing transactions build on several major project-level funding milestones completed during 2026.
In May, Rowan secured approximately $2.9 billion for its 300-megawatt Temple data center campus.
The transaction represented the largest financing in the company’s history and was completed under Rowan’s Green Finance Framework.
Earlier in February, the company obtained $550 million in construction financing for its 300-megawatt Cinco campus in Medina County, Texas.

SAN FRANCISCO , Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Today, we're announcing that we've raised $1B in a Series A, led by Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital, with participation from Battery Ventures, Doerr Capital, Gil & Co, Google, M13, Pear VC, and S32, among other new and existing investors.
We believe making AI R&D more accessible is the most direct path to AI that solves humanity's most pressing problems across science and technology. We're building tools to democratize frontier AI R&D and help put it within reach of every scientist and engineer.
Over the past three weeks, we've shared our first results, and they point to the same shift: when agents do the hands-on work, the size of your team stops limiting what you can build. One researcher, working with agents, pretrained Mirendil-Base , a competitive coding model, from scratch in 3.5 months with less than $10M in compute. We then post-trained it into Fern , which holds up to 10M tokens of context, enough for days of an agent's work. The inaugural AI 100 recognizes leading private companies driving innovation across the AI ecosystem. Positron's inclusion reflects its progress in bringing purpose-built inference technology to market as growing AI adoption drives demand for more cost- and energy-efficient infrastructure.
"We're honored to be recognized among the companies shaping the future of AI," said Mitesh Agrawal, CEO of Positron AI. "Making AI inference profitable, scalable and accessible takes advanced technology and a business and supply chain built to serve some of the world's largest technology companies. Positron combines deep semiconductor and systems expertise with customer-driven development and investor backing to position us for growth. I'm proud of the business we're building as we serve customers today and develop our next generation of technology, and grateful to our team, customers, partners and investors for their support."
Positron's recognition follows a series of major company milestones. In September, the company announced an $875 million Series C financing at a $5 billion valuation to accelerate development of its next-generation Asimov silicon, ramp production of Titan and expand manufacturing capacity. Positron has also deployed more than 50 racks of Atlas, its first-generation inference system, at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. Most recently, the company announced a partnership with General Compute, which is purchasing Atlas systems and has committed to adopting Titan to support next-generation AI workloads.
The inaugural AI 100 evaluated nominated companies and recognized category leaders across four factors: market leadership (35%), estimated valuation (30%), operating metrics (20%), and people & culture (15%). Only independent AI companies that have not had a majority strategic or private equity M&A transaction or a public listing were eligible. Honorees span foundation models, AI infrastructure and compute, developer tools and agents, AI apps, vertical AI, security, physical AI and robotics, and deeptech and AI for science.

Ukraine-founded defense technology company Uforce has raised $700 million in Series A funding at a $6 billion valuation to expand production of autonomous military systems for Ukraine and allied nations.
The round was co-led by Valor Equity Partners and the UK National Wealth Fund, with participation from the U.S.-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund, according to Uforce . Other investors included Menlo Ventures , Xantium and Hiro Capital, while existing backers Shield Capital , Ballistic Ventures , Lakestar and Squadra increased their stakes.
Headquartered in London, with major operations in Kyiv and Washington, Uforce develops uncrewed systems for air, land and sea operations, along with AI software for coordinating and controlling them. The company said the funding will support manufacturing expansion across the United States, Europe, Asia-Pacific and the Middle East, while maintaining production and supplies for Ukrainian forces despite continued attacks in Ukraine.
Expanding Autonomous Defense Production
Uforce plans to increase production and research and development across four product families: MAGURA uncrewed surface vessels, NEMESIS aerial drones, LIUT ground vehicles and PREDATOR turret systems.
The company also anticipates working with partners in allied countries to adapt existing maritime and automotive manufacturing facilities for defense production.
Uforce recently announced a partnership with ReconCraft to expand U.S. manufacturing of its Maritime Autonomous Guard Unmanned Robotic Apparatus (MAGURA) vessels. It also plans to build on relationships within NATO and Joint Expeditionary Force networks and continue participating as a founding member of the EU-Ukraine Drone Alliance.
CEO Oleg Rogynskyy said the financing will help increase production for Ukraine while providing allied nations with autonomous systems they can deploy, integrate and maintain.
“The war in Ukraine has shown that in an increasingly volatile world, effective defense requires systems that can keep improving as threats change,” noted Rogynskyy. “Governments and the technology ecosystem need to come together to develop cost-effective, interoperable, and autonomous platforms that are ready to fight now, and can evolve to meet future needs.”
Investment Supports Ukrainian Operations
The U.S.-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund’s participation will specifically support Uforce’s operations in Ukraine, including staffing, research and development, and new products. The fund was established jointly by the United States and Ukraine to attract investment into reconstruction, economic development and strategic industries.
Uforce also announced that retired Gen. Christopher G. Cavoli, former NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe and a partner at Valor Equity Partners, will join its board of directors.

Torus, a Salt Lake City energy infrastructure manufacturer, launched Foundry, a prefabricated modular AI compute system, and raised $500 million in growth capital led by Magnetar on Nov. 11. Participating investors include ICONIQ, Origin Ventures, Ridgeline Partners and Trinity Capital.
Foundry packages power, storage, cooling, networking and compute into a single modular unit that installs at existing commercial and industrial sites in 12 to 16 weeks, a fraction of the multiyear timeline typical for a hyperscale data center campus. Each site delivers 1 to 20 megawatts of capacity, with the smallest unit roughly the size of a cargo van. The system taps spare grid capacity that utilities have already allocated to existing sites, avoiding the infrastructure upgrades that often trigger rate increases.
The raise follows a $200 million investment from Magnetar in September 2025 , making this the second nine-figure investment the Evanston, Illinois-based asset manager has made in Torus in just over a year.
Betting on inference over training
The launch targets a shift in AI economics: Data center demand for inference, the process of running trained models rather than building them, is projected to grow at a 35% compound annual rate through 2030, compared with 22% for training, according to McKinsey . Unlike training, inference runs continuously and benefits from sitting close to users, pulling demand toward smaller, distributed sites rather than centralized campuses.
“Most providers are bringing power to the chips. Foundry brings the chips to power,” says Nate Walkingshaw, founder and CEO of Torus, who previously served as chief experience officer at Pluralsight before founding Torus in 2021.
“One of the biggest challenges in scaling AI infrastructure is access to power, and the solution isn’t simply generating more of it, but making better use of what’s already available,” says Dave Snyderman, managing partner and global head of alternative credit and fixed income at Magnetar. “Torus has spent years building the energy infrastructure and expertise to address this challenge. Foundry builds on that foundation by bringing compute to available power, helping unlock capacity within the existing grid.”
Photo courtesy of Torus
Foundry ships in three configurations: a powered shell without GPUs, a turnkey bare-metal unit with GPUs included, and a single-tenant sovereign model for enterprises that want exclusive hardware. Torus launched the product with its first customers, bare-metal GPU cloud provider Hydra Host and an unnamed AI cloud provider, and plans to have more than 47,000 GPUs running in Foundry units by the end of 2027.
Manufacturing scale in Utah
Foundry units are built at GigaOne, Torus’s 545,000-square-foot manufacturing facility in Salt Lake City, where the company employs nearly 400 people. GigaOne opened its first production line in early 2026 and added a new line roughly every 21 days through the year; the Foundry line is online and expected to reach 500 megawatts of IT load, with plans to expand to 1 gigawatt.
The $500 million will fund continued expansion of GigaOne along with Torus Reserve and Foundry deployments nationwide. The company says each Foundry unit uses a waterless closed-loop cooling system that requires no water or sewer connection and donates GPU time to medical research through Folding@home.

VulcanForms announces $500M financing agreement
VulcanForms plans to build three factories by the end of 2027, fueled by a $500 million financing deal the company announced Thursday. Photo I Courtesy VulcanForms
By Paula J. Owen
November 13, 2026

VulcanForms plans to build three factories by the end of 2027 including one in Massachusetts, fueled by a $500 million financing deal the company announced Thursday.
“Factory No. 4” is planned for Massachusetts, according to VulcanForms CEO Kevin Kassekert, who confirmed the company also plans to double its workforce to approximately 1,000 by the end of 2027.
The financing, led by J.P. Morgan and Apollo-managed funds, supports three additional factories by the metal parts manufacturer that has existing operations in Newburyport and two in Devens where it is adding 1 million square-feet of manufacturing space .
VulcanForms, a pioneer in advanced digital manufacturing, said it plans to use the funding to accelerate the next phase of American industrial production.
Backed by multibillion-dollar commercial programs across critical industries, VulcanForms said it is expanding to meet growing customer demand, marking a milestone in the company’s transition from breakthrough manufacturing technology to industrial-scale production, according to a press release.
ADVERTISEMENT
As American industries seek to strengthen domestic production and reduce dependence on fragmented global supply chains, the challenge extends beyond technological innovation to manufacturing complex, high-performance components at the scale, speed and cost required to compete globally, the company said.
VulcanForms is addressing the challenge through a fully integrated digital manufacturing platform that combines metal additive manufacturing, precision machining, automation and physical AI.
By unifying traditionally fragmented production processes, the company is establishing a new model for producing critical components competitively in the U.S., it says.
Kevin Kassekert, CEO of VulcanForms Photo I Courtesy VulcanForms
“America cannot lead the next industrial revolution if we can’t manufacture what we invent,” Kassekert said. “For too long, breakthrough technologies developed here have been manufactured overseas.
ADVERTISEMENT
“VulcanForms is proving we can change that by turning American innovation into industrial-scale production and demonstrating that the U.S. can not only compete, but also win on the global stage. We’re proud to work with J.P. Morgan and Apollo on helping to build America’s industrial future at home.”
VulcanForms uses advanced 3D printing and machining to make complex metal parts for industries like aerospace, medical and defense. The company has presented itself as part of an effort to reshore manufacturing and to secure domestic supply chains.
The firm was awarded $21.26 million in tax credits from the Massachusetts Economic Assistance Coordinating Council to support the construction of a 1-million-square-foot advanced manufacturing facility in Devens.
The expansion is part of an effort to establish a multi-facility VulcanForms campus in Devens, according to ConnectCRE.com .
ADVERTISEMENT
VulcanForms has secured multibillion-dollar commercial programs spanning medical devices, consumer products, aerospace, defense, space and industrial markets, demonstrating significant demand for its integrated manufacturing platform.
VulcanForms was founded out of MIT in 2015. The firm works with clients to design parts and manufacture them in its own facilities, seeking to minimize sourcing of raw materials from overseas.
The company has secured multibillion-dollar commercial programs across critical industries, raising over $1 billion in funding since its launch including $220 million in January that included a contribution from Florida-based 1789 Capital , a venture capital firm whose partners include Donald Trump Jr.

Peak 10 Energy: $500 Million Facility To Finance Oil And Gas Acquisitions
By Amit Chowdhry
Nov 12, 2026
Peak 10 Energy: $500 Million Facility To Finance Oil And Gas Acquisitions
Peak 10 Energy has established a financing partnership with U.S. Bank that provides as much as $500 million for acquisitions of producing oil and gas assets across the U.S.
The acquisition finance facility will support Peak 10’s strategy of consolidating packages weighted toward proved developed producing properties. These assets have established production and can generate more predictable cash flows than undeveloped acreage.
U.S. Bank structured the facility to support later asset-backed securities issuances. That approach could provide longer-term institutional financing after Peak 10 completes and assembles acquisitions.
Peak 10 was founded in 2023 and has completed 12 acquisition and divestiture transactions involving operated properties, non-operated interests, and mineral assets across U.S. onshore basins.
The new facility will allow the company to pursue larger transactions and close acquisitions more quickly. Peak 10 said it encountered additional opportunities during 2026 that it could have acquired if the facility had already been available.
The company also maintains a commodity hedging relationship with U.S. Bank. Hedging can help stabilize cash flow from acquired properties and support financing by reducing exposure to oil and gas price volatility.
Peak 10’s strategy focuses on extending the productive lives of existing fields and infrastructure. The company expects this approach to support domestic energy production without depending solely on new exploration.
Legacy Star Capital Partners backs Peak 10 and views the combination of producing-asset consolidation and asset-backed financing as a long-duration investment strategy.
Petrie Partners originated the transaction and advised Peak 10. Baker Botts served as Peak 10’s legal adviser, while Haynes Boone represented U.S. Bank.
KEY QUOTES
“This facility and our commodity hedging relationship with U.S. Bank give us the financial firepower to close acquisitions at a scale that matches the opportunity we see in the market.”
Kyle McQuire, Chief Executive Officer of Peak 10 Energy
“The ABS structure provides a durable source of capital, and reflects the practical, solutions-oriented approach our structured lending team brings to help clients achieve their objectives.”
William Eustis, Co-Head of Asset-Backed Securities at U.S. Bank

Ballistic Ventures: $490 Million Fundraising Target For Two New Cybersecurity Funds Amid AI Security Boom
Ballistic Ventures, a San Francisco-based venture capital firm specializing in cybersecurity investments, is seeking to raise $490 million across two new investment funds as artificial intelligence drives demand for technologies that protect businesses against increasingly sophisticated cyber threats. According to a TechCrunch report , the firm has filed documents with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission seeking $360 million for its third flagship fund and an additional $130 million for a separate investment vehicle called Ballistic Ventures Fund B.
The regulatory filings indicate that neither fund had recorded any capital sales at the time of submission, meaning the amounts represent fundraising targets rather than completed capital commitments.

Ballistic Ventures was founded in late 2021 by a team of experienced cybersecurity executives and investors.
Its founding team includes Ted Schlein, a former partner at Kleiner Perkins, where he spent more than two decades investing in technology companies.
Other founders include Barmak Meftah, former President of AT&T Cybersecurity, and Roger Thornton, who co-founded cybersecurity companies Fortify Software and AlienVault.
The firm’s leadership brings experience in cybersecurity company development, enterprise software, and venture capital investing.

Its approach emphasizes identifying companies developing technologies designed to address evolving security challenges.
The firm has developed a portfolio spanning enterprise security, AI-related threats, and other cybersecurity applications.

Its portfolio includes Talon Cyber Security, which was acquired by Palo Alto Networks.
The firm also invested in Pangea, a security company acquired by CrowdStrike.
These transactions illustrate Ballistic Ventures’ participation in companies developing technologies attractive to established cybersecurity vendors.
Other portfolio companies include Armadin, GetReal, Nudge Security, and Oligo Security.
The businesses operate across different areas of cybersecurity, reflecting the firm’s interest in emerging security requirements.
Ballistic Ventures’ investments also provide exposure to technologies designed to help organizations manage risks associated with increasingly complex software and IT environments.
The firm’s potential new funds would build on its existing portfolio and investment strategy.

AI applications can help businesses automate workflows and improve operational efficiency, but they can also create new vulnerabilities.
The growing deployment of autonomous AI agents introduces additional security considerations because these systems may interact with sensitive information, enterprise applications, and external services.
Organizations are increasingly evaluating security technologies that can monitor AI activity, control access to critical systems, and protect proprietary information.
At the same time, attackers are using AI to increase the speed and scale of malicious activities.
Microsoft’s October 2026 Digital Defense Report warned that cybercriminals are increasingly using AI for phishing, social engineering, and malware development.
Although many underlying attack techniques remain familiar, AI can make them easier to execute at greater volume.
These developments are creating opportunities for cybersecurity startups developing new defensive technologies.

Investors are backing companies developing AI-powered threat detection, automated security operations, and technologies intended to protect AI applications themselves.

By Amit Chowdhry
Yesterday at 1:35 PM
Viasat: $450 Million U.S. Space Force Contract For Golden Dome Space Data Network Backbone Development
Viasat, a Carlsbad, California-based provider of satellite communications and secure networking technologies, has received an indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity (IDIQ) contract with a ceiling of $450 million from the U.S. Space Force’s Space Systems Command (SSC). The award will support the development, deployment, sustainment, and operation of the Space Data Network Backbone (SDN-B) mission operations center, a critical component of the military’s efforts to establish resilient space-based communications infrastructure supporting Golden Dome for America and Joint Force operations.
The contract includes an initial $115 million task order to support development and scaling of the mission operations center and associated network operations capabilities.
The $450 million represents the maximum value available under the IDIQ contract rather than a guaranteed payment to Viasat. Additional work will depend on future task orders and government requirements.
The award positions Viasat as a network and mission systems integration partner supporting the Space Force’s efforts to establish a more interconnected and resilient military space architecture.
The SDN-B initiative is designed to provide high-capacity, low-latency data transport across multiple satellite networks and orbital environments.
Its architecture will support communications requirements for the U.S. Space Force, Golden Dome for America, and military operations conducted by the Joint Force worldwide.
Supporting The Golden Dome Space Data Network Backbone
The Space Data Network Backbone is a multi-vendor data transport architecture designed to connect and manage communications capabilities across participating space and ground systems.
The network is intended to provide resilient connectivity for military operations that depend on timely access to information collected and transmitted through space-based infrastructure.
Rather than relying on a single satellite operator or communications architecture, SDN-B is designed to integrate multiple providers and network elements.
This approach supports the Space Force’s broader objective of developing open architectures that can incorporate commercial technologies and adapt to changing mission requirements.
Viasat will focus on the mission operations center responsible for supporting network management and integration under government direction.
The center is intended to provide a coordinated view of participating SDN-B network elements, allowing operators to monitor connectivity, network performance, and operational status.
The infrastructure will also support government-directed prioritization of communications resources based on military mission requirements.
$115 Million Initial Task Order
The initial $115 million task order will fund work associated with establishing and scaling the SDN-B mission operations center and its network operations capabilities.
Viasat will apply its experience operating secure satellite communications networks to support the development of an enterprise-level operational infrastructure.
The company’s responsibilities include systems engineering, network integration, operational support, and sustainment activities.
The mission operations center will provide tools to manage participating connectivity services and support a common operational picture of the network.
These capabilities are intended to help military operators understand the status and performance of the communications infrastructure supporting their missions.
The contract also provides a framework for future engineering, operational, and sustainment work as the SDN-B architecture develops.
Additional task orders may support evolving requirements involving network availability, cybersecurity, and resilience.
Systems Engineering And Multi-Orbit Integration
A major component of Viasat’s responsibilities involves systems engineering and integration across space-to-ground communications interfaces.
The company will support the integration of multi-orbit connectivity services, helping participating satellite systems operate within a coordinated network architecture.
Multi-orbit communications can involve satellites operating at different altitudes, each with distinct characteristics involving coverage, latency, and available capacity.
Integrating these services can provide military communications planners with greater flexibility and resilience.
Viasat will also help establish enterprise network operations infrastructure to support the management of data transport services.
These capabilities will operate according to government-directed mission priorities.
The objective is to create an integrated operational environment capable of coordinating communications resources across multiple providers.

This capability is intended to help operators monitor network conditions and maintain awareness of participating SDN-B elements.

These activities will be performed according to government requirements and applicable future task orders.
The sustainment effort will address evolving needs involving network availability, operational resilience, and cybersecurity.

Zilch: £395 Million Debt Facilities Expand Consumer Lending Capacity
By Amit Chowdhry
Nov 12, 2026
Zilch: £395 Million Debt Facilities Expand Consumer Lending Capacity
Zilch has increased its securitization and corporate debt facilities by £165 million, bringing total commitments to £395 million as the payments company expands its product offering. Deutsche Bank led the latest financing, with participation from two major credit funds. The facilities will enable Zilch to originate up to £6 billion in lending annually.
The additional capacity supports customer growth and demand for products including Pay Monthly, launched in August 2026. That offering allows qualifying customers to spread purchases over three, six or 12 months.
Zilch is targeting a broader range of spending needs, including larger purchases such as holidays, household appliances and insurance premiums.
Average annual spending per active customer has reached £2,500, while the company’s gross merchandise value run rate has exceeded £3.5 billion.
The financing follows Zilch’s announcement that it surpassed a $300 million annual run rate and recorded two consecutive quarters of adjusted profit before tax in its 2027 financial year.
The company also plans to move into a new London headquarters in spring 2027, more than doubling its office capacity.
Founded in 2018, Zilch combines debit, credit, installments, earned wage access, credit-building features, offers and rewards within its payments platform.
The expanded funding facilities provide more lending capacity as that product mix develops. Management identified access to efficient funding as important to supporting higher transaction volumes and continued growth.
Chief Financial Officer Hugh Courtney said the financing reflects funders’ confidence in Zilch’s underwriting and ability to scale profitably in the United Kingdom.
The company’s strategy is to serve more customer payment needs through the same platform, strengthening engagement as users move between everyday spending and larger purchases.
KEY QUOTES:
“As we continue to grow at significant scale, having access to efficient funding is a key parameter for success. These expanded facilities give us greater capacity to support our customers where they need us, capturing more of the transactions that matter to customers day to day and providing the most rewarding ways to pay. By serving a broader range of customer needs, we can continue building a highly engaged customer relationship and delivering the value, flexibility and features that our customers really want.”
Philip Belamant, CEO And Co-Founder Of Zilch

candidates.title: Exus Closes $345 Million Financing Led by Goldman Sachs Alternatives
candidates.snippet: Exus Closes $345 Million Financing Led by Goldman Sachs Alternatives Hoodline
candidates.text:
Source: Nikki / Wikimedia Commons
Exus Renewables North America said Thursday it closed $345 million in senior secured holding company financing led by Goldman Sachs Alternatives, money the company says will go toward construction and new U.S. wind, solar and battery projects.
The check is another in a run of company financings and project deals, not a map of which turbines or panels get the cash. Exus framed the close against rising U.S. electricity demand and described itself as an independent owner, developer and operator of utility-scale renewable energy and storage.
What the Money Is For
Exus said the financing will support construction costs and development across its growing U.S. portfolio of wind, solar and battery storage assets. The announcement does not name the projects that will draw on the facility or split the dollars among those three technologies.
President and CEO Jim Spencer said the financing lets the company keep its momentum going. He also said Goldman Sachs Alternatives' support reflects confidence in Exus and gives it flexibility to build projects and bring generation online, including work already underway and a deeper pipeline.
Vikas Agrawal, managing director and co-head of Energy Transition Climate Credit at Goldman Sachs Alternatives, said Exus has a strong platform for developing and operating utility-scale renewable projects. "We're pleased to support its continued investment in new energy infrastructure," he said, tying that support to growing U.S. electricity demand.
A Larger Company-Reported Book
Exus reported more than 800 megawatts operating or under construction and a total portfolio exceeding 6 gigawatts. Those are company figures, not an outside audit of nameplate capacity.
The comparison that is on the record is Exus' own July 22, 2025 financing announcement. Then, the company reported more than 5 gigawatts in its total portfolio and 764 megawatts operating or under construction, alongside $308.2 million in financing for the 185-megawatt Zia Solar portfolio in New Mexico and the 169-megawatt Keystone wind portfolio in Pennsylvania.
From that July 2025 snapshot to Thursday's release, the company-reported operating-or-under-construction figure moved from 764 megawatts to more than 800, and the total portfolio from over 5 gigawatts to more than 6. Exus also said it is expanding its operational footprint to meet growing national energy needs, with work that includes developing, repowering and managing renewable assets.
Separate Deals, Not One Stack
This holding-company financing sits beside other Exus transactions that the available reporting treats as separate. pv magazine USA reported in January that Exus had closed a $400 million senior secured corporate credit facility tied to a 4.5-gigawatt pipeline. Nothing in the Thursday announcement establishes whether that facility is still outstanding or how it relates to the $345 million.
Project-level money has also moved on its own track. On Sept. 22, Exus said it had completed the Highland North and Cambria wind repower projects in Cambria County, Pennsylvania, and that construction was financed through roughly $356 million led by KeyBanc Capital Markets. A week later, on Sept. 29, Exus and ibV Energy Partners announced that Exus had acquired four solar projects totaling 715 megawatts-peak.
Those deals show a company adding and rebuilding capacity in named places — Cambria County wind, a New Mexico solar book, Pennsylvania wind — while Thursday's $345 million is described only at the holding-company level.
Demand, Offices and the Close
Exus put the financing in a market it describes as tight on power. In the Cambria County release, the company said demand for clean power from data centers and other large energy users keeps climbing across that region. Nationally, a Jan. 13 Energy Information Administration release forecast the strongest four-year growth in U.S. electricity demand since 2000, fueled by data centers, and said solar would supply the largest increase in power generation, up a forecast 21% in both 2026 and 2027 after almost 70 gigawatts of new capacity. That is a forecast, not a reading of what Exus will actually build.
The company said it has more than 110 employees operating from offices in Pittsburgh, New York, Albuquerque and Connecticut. PEI Global Partners was financial advisor to Exus. Latham & Watkins LLP was legal counsel to Exus, and Vinson & Elkins LLP was legal counsel to Goldman Sachs Alternatives.
What Thursday actually puts on the table is $345 million of senior secured holding-company financing, led by Goldman Sachs Alternatives, for construction costs and new wind, solar and storage development — with the project list still unstated.

candidates.title: LangChain Raises $300M Series C at a $3B Valuation Led by CapitalG
candidates.snippet: LangChain Raises $300M Series C at a $3B Valuation Led by CapitalG Wowtale
candidates.text:
AI agents are moving out of experiments and into day-to-day work, and building, running and watching them has become a new problem for companies. Picking a model is not enough. Teams need to trace why an agent got something wrong, catch performance slipping in production, and control which tools and data it can reach. LangChain , whose platform targets exactly that, has raised $300 million in a Series C.
From open-source framework to agent engineering platform
LangChain says its mission is to help every company own its intelligence. As agents transform the economy, it says, companies are building domain-specific agents differentiated by their knowledge, data and user experience, and the companies that control them will gain lasting advantages.
The product centers on LangSmith and rests on three pillars. Agent Runtime covers running agents reliably. Deep Agents, LangGraph and LangChain give developers flexibility across models and control over context. LangSmith Agent Server and Sandboxes deploy agents securely at scale in the cloud or a customer’s own environment, and Managed Agents and Fleet run mission-critical agents as managed services. Agent Improvement covers testing and monitoring. Observability and Evaluation show how agents behave and measure quality, and LangSmith Engine, an in-platform agent, finds errors, writes code and prompt fixes and watches production traffic for regressions. Fine-Tuning turns traces into training data for specialized models. Agent Governance gives central control over models, tools and data. LLM and Tool Gateways manage model budgets and fallbacks, protect sensitive data, and govern tool access and authentication.
More than 7,000 organizations already use LangSmith, according to LangChain, from fast-growing startups such as Harvey , Rippling and Listen Labs to Fortune 500 enterprises such as Nvidia , Toyota and Salesforce . Clay uses it to monitor hundreds of millions of agent runs a month. Workday uses it to run and govern agents across the organization, cutting the time to deploy a new agent from five months to under a day. These figures come from the company and have not been independently verified.
A side project that started weeks after ChatGPT
LangChain began within weeks of ChatGPT’s release in late 2022. Harrison Chase , then an engineer at Robust Intelligence, started it as a personal open-source project to fix a gap in large language models: they could not reach live information or take real actions such as web search or API calls. After founding the company with Ankush Gola, he raised a $10 million seed led by Benchmark in April 2023 and a $25 million Series A led by Sequoia in February 2024, at a $200 million valuation.
Valuation more than doubles in a year
LangChain said on Nov. 13 that it raised $300 million at a $3 billion valuation, bringing total funding to $460 million. Existing investor CapitalG led, with significant participation from new investors GIC and DFJ Growth and existing investors IVP and Sapphire Ventures .
New investors also include Salesforce Ventures , Insight Partners , QuantumLight and MongoDB Ventures, and existing investors Sequoia , Amplify and Benchmark returned. LangChain became a unicorn last October with a $125 million Series B at a $1.25 billion valuation, so its valuation has more than doubled in about a year.
Mo Jomaa, a partner at CapitalG, said the shift from experimental LLM applications to production-grade agents is among the most significant in enterprise software today. He said Chase and his team have built a foundational platform for agent engineering and earned the trust of thousands of developers and global enterprises. LangChain will show new LangSmith capabilities at a special release event on Nov. 20.
Competitors
In observability, Braintrust is a leading name. It measures and evaluates how AI models and agents behave in production, and raised an $80 million Series B in February at an $800 million valuation, led by ICONIQ. Langfuse , an open-source LLM observability platform, was acquired by ClickHouse in January, the same day ClickHouse announced a $400 million Series D at a $15 billion valuation.
On the development side, LlamaIndex builds an agent platform around unstructured data and raised a $19 million Series A led by Norwest Venture Partners in March 2025. Temporal , a durable-execution platform that keeps long-running agents going after interruptions, raised $550 million in a Series E in September.

candidates.title: Welding AI Maker Path Robotics Raises $300M Series E With NAVER Ventures
candidates.snippet: Welding AI Maker Path Robotics Raises $300M Series E With NAVER Ventures Wowtale
candidates.text:
Skilled welders are hard to find, and shipyards and heavy-equipment plants are sitting on full order books. Traditional industrial robots do not help much here. They follow pre-programmed paths, which makes them a poor fit for welds that differ slightly from one part to the next. Path Robotics , a Columbus, Ohio-based startup, is betting that a robot that can see and decide for itself can fill that gap. On Nov. 10, the company announced a $300 million Series E at a $2.45 billion post-money valuation.
Georgian , an AI-focused growth equity firm, led the round. NAVER Ventures and D. E. Shaw Ventures joined as new investors, and existing backers Addition, Drive Capital, IronArc Ventures, Tiger Global, and Yamaha Motor Ventures also took part. Georgian partner Emily Walsh will join Path’s board.
Giving the robot eyes and judgment
A conventional welding robot has to be taught its path step by step, and a part that sits slightly out of place can ruin the weld. Path’s physical AI welding model, Obsidian, takes that teaching out of the loop. The robot finds the weld joint on its own, plans the sequence and path, welds, and adjusts when conditions change mid-job. The model learns from real-world welding data. For a factory, that means variable welds without reprogramming the robot each time.
The company recently added Rove, a mobile welding system that puts Obsidian on a quadruped robot. Instead of bringing the part to a welding cell, the robot walks to the part. Path says it shows the same model can run on different robot bodies.
ARR up 17x in 18 months, led by shipbuilding and defense
Path says its annual recurring revenue grew 17-fold over the past 18 months, though it did not disclose a dollar figure. The growth has come from shipbuilding and defense, heavy equipment, and energy infrastructure. Customers include HII, the largest U.S. shipbuilder, Lockheed Martin, and the maritime defense company Saronic , along with mid-sized manufacturers such as EK Machine, Millerbernd Manufacturing, TransAmerican Power Products, and TYCROP. Earlier this year, Path announced a $600 million performance-based production agreement with HII to deploy physical AI across U.S. Navy shipbuilding programs. Headcount has grown 97% over the past year, and the company plans to reach 400 employees by year-end.
CEO and co-founder Andy Lonsberry said Path started with welding because it is one of the hardest jobs on the factory floor to automate. “Our goal isn’t to automate one step, but to automate the entire factory,” he said. Founded in 2018, Path has now raised more than $610 million. The new money will go toward scaling the welding business, expanding to tasks before and after welding and to new robot form factors, and training AI models.
Georgian pointed to Path’s proprietary models and its growing base of production data, which it said improves the system with every deployment. Lockheed Martin Ventures called the investment an important milestone for strengthening the U.S. defense industrial base.
Competition: welding specialists and general-purpose robot AI
A handful of newer companies are going after the same problem. Korea’s RB-Ware makes a no-code welding robot and has installed more than 250 units in 16 countries, and NeoArcRobotics is building cutting and welding robots for Korean shipyards. Augmentus raised $11 million to scale physical AI for robotic welding, and China’s LE Robotics raised tens of millions of yuan in a Series A+ round in February. None has raised anything close to Path’s total.
Others are chasing general-purpose robot intelligence rather than one task. Skild AI and Physical Intelligence are building foundation models meant to run on any robot, and defense manufacturer Hadrian raised $1.37 billion in a Series D in August to rebuild U.S. manufacturing capacity. Where those companies bet on a universal model or on the factory itself, Path is trying to perfect the hardest single process first and then extend to the steps around it.

Windward Bio Group priced its initial public offering of 10,294,117 shares at $17 each on Nov. 12, the midpoint of its $16 to $18 range, and sold an additional $50 million of shares and pre-funded warrants to Sanofi in a concurrent private placement at the same price [1] [5] . Gross proceeds are expected to total $225 million before fees and before the underwriters' option on 1,544,117 more shares [1] . The stock began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on Friday under the symbol WWB, and the deal is set to close on Nov. 16 [1] .
Boston-based Rezera postponed a planned $200 million IPO on the evening of Nov. 11, citing market conditions, according to IPOScoop [4] . Jefferies and TD Cowen were bookrunners on both deals, alongside Piper Sandler and UBS for Windward and Cantor Fitzgerald for Rezera [1] [3] .
Two drugs licensed from China
Windward, formed two years ago, raised $365 million of venture funding before the IPO [2] . Its lead drug, WIN378, is an ultra-long-acting injectable that blocks TSLP, the same inflammatory protein targeted by AstraZeneca and Amgen's Tezspire, and could be dosed as rarely as twice a year against Tezspire's monthly schedule [2] . Windward licensed it from Kelun Biotech, which co-developed it with Harbour BioMed [2] . The Phase 3 part of an asthma trial began in September with results expected next year, and a mid-stage COPD study started in June with data due in 2027 [2] . A second drug, WIN027, licensed from Qyuns Therapeutics, targets both TSLP and IL-13 [2] . Windward paid $70 million upfront in cash and equity for the two programs and owes up to $1.6 billion more in milestone payments [2] .
Windward is the biotech sector's 30th IPO this year, according to BioPharma Dive, which counts 2026 as the busiest year for drugmaker listings since 2021, with more than $8 billion raised [2] .
Rezera steps back
Rezera, formerly NodThera, develops oral NLRP3 inhibitors for inflammatory diseases and describes itself as Phase 3-ready [3] [4] . It had planned to sell 16.7 million shares at $11 to $13 on the Nasdaq under the symbol RZRA, and GSK had indicated interest in buying up to $25 million of the offering, about 13% of the deal [3] . Its last amended registration statement was filed with the SEC on Nov. 9 [6] . The company has not said when it might return. The postponement came in the same week that Anthropic's bankers weighed pricing its IPO above its marketed range.

candidates.title: Midwest startups raise $213.5 million in a week. Where is the money going?
candidates.snippet: Midwest startups raise $213.5 million in a week. Where is the money going? Techli
candidates.text:
Four of six deals are reported in Chicago, and the region is experiencing the latest funding activity in the form of investments in AI infrastructure and financial services.
According to StartMidwest’s funding roundup , $213.5 million was raised in six deals by Midwest startups and financial technology companies during the week ending Nov. 6, with two $100 million rounds accounting for almost all the capital.
Ocient, an AI infrastructure firm in Chicago, and Erebor Bank, which is based in Columbus, Ohio, were the leaders of the activity. The remaining included health care technology, artificial intelligence and fintech firms, reflecting the diversity of sectors that are being invested in all over the region.
The headline figure, however, requires some qualification: Erebor Bank’s $100 million investment from Japan’s SBI Holdings was announced as a planned commitment, not a completed financing round. The difference is important in evaluating the amount of capital that actually has flowed to companies in the Midwest.
The biggest round up to date was Ocient’s $100 million Series C , which was announced on November 5. The investment, led by BOKA Capital and OCA Ventures, totals $260 million for the Chicago firm. Other investors who were on board included existing investors Greycroft, In-Q-Tel, Blue Bear Capital, Buoyant Ventures, PSP Growth, Pritzker Group Venture Capital and Eron Wolf. Dallas Venture Capital joined as a new investor.
Ocient is a company that creates data analytics and AI solutions for enterprises dealing with vast amounts of data. The new investment will allow it to continue developing its OcientAIQ solutions that enable enterprises to deploy AI agents and analytics in petabyte-scale data environments.
Reliable, governed data is becoming a key infrastructure need as businesses delve into agentic AI systems that can analyze information and execute tasks. Ocient claims its solution can be used for data governance along with high-performance data analytics, enabling AI agents and analysts to ask questions about the data in a customer’s environment.
The company anticipates that its revenue will more than triple in 2026 due to the demand of customers with growing and high-volume data sets. This projection is not a financial result but an estimate by Ocient.
The second $100 million was from a digital bank called Erebor Bank, based in Columbus, Ohio, which offers services to companies in fields such as artificial intelligence, robotics and advanced manufacturing, defense, and energy. The timing of the completion of the investment was not mentioned in the funding roundup, but SBI Holdings revealed its plan to invest $100 million .
Four of the six transactions were in Chicago. In addition to Ocient, medical technology firm Focused Medical Technologies, a treatment developer for pulmonary embolism, secured $6 million in investment, including two medical technology strategic investors and UCM Ventures. The University of Chicago startup is targeting the funds for product development, manufacturing and setting up for a pivotal study in the United States.
Consumer insights firm QualSights raised $5 million in funding, led by Duo Partners. The company employs smart sensors and a consumer application and AI analytics to provide a better understanding of how humans use physical products. The funding came with the appointment of Prasanna Pitale as Chief Executive.
Fifth Star Funds and Chicago Early Growth Ventures joined Izou Partners as the lead investors in an oversubscribed $2.5 million pre-seed round for healthcare technology company CareLumi. Its software will track AI-powered and automated workflows in healthcare delivery systems, starting with provider credentialing and payer enrollment.
Minneapolis-based Duome capped the list with a capital investment from Great Lakes Credit Union. The company is connecting with credit unions to assist homebuyers who meet the qualifications to acquire homes using a co-investment approach.
The four of the deals occurred in Chicago, Columbus, and Minneapolis, each had one deal. The sector split also indicates that the regions aren’t just focused on traditional software startups – the financial services, health care, and AI infrastructure sectors are also included.
Nevertheless, the weekly total was very skewed. The two $100 million deals made up about 94% of the total $213.5 million reported, with the remaining four deals making up a much smaller portion of the total.
The numbers indicate ongoing investor interest in tackling complex challenges in infrastructure and industry-specific issues for the Midwest startup ecosystem. However, the size disparity between these large financing announcements and the smaller rounds at the early stage also poses a question for the region: Is it possible to reliably get capital to startups at various stages of development?

Patrick Industries ( PATK ) announced on November 13, 2026 that its board had increased the quarterly common-stock dividend to $0.52 per share from $0.47 and replenished its share-repurchase authorization to $200 million. The announcement pairs a higher cash payout with additional repurchase capacity that cannot currently be used because of covenants in Patrick’s pending all-stock merger with LCI Industries ( LCII ) .
The board approved the dividend increase on November 11, 2026. The new rate is approximately 10.6% above the previous rate, calculated from the announced per-share amounts. The dividend is payable on December 7, 2026, to shareholders of record at the close of business on November 23, 2026.
Repurchase Capacity Remains Restricted
The authorization covers repurchases over the next 24 months and includes $61.9 million that remained under the previous authorization. The board therefore added $138.1 million of capacity, calculated as the difference between the new total and the remaining amount.
The repurchase program cannot presently be used. Patrick entered into the LCI merger agreement on June 30, 2026, and its operating covenants restrict repurchases of Patrick common stock. The company expects those restrictions to remain in place while the agreement is in effect.
The restrictions were already visible in Patrick’s third-quarter report , which said the company made no share repurchases during the quarter because of the merger agreement. The SEC declared the merger registration statement effective on October 19, 2026, and Patrick has scheduled a special shareholder meeting for November 18, 2026.
Cash Flow and Capital Allocation
Chief Executive Officer Andy Nemeth said the decisions were grounded in Patrick’s capital allocation, cash generation and balance sheet. “Since initiating our quarterly dividend in 2019, we have raised it each year and have been active with share repurchases, deploying $106.1 million in the first nine months of 2026,” he said.
Returning capital is only one use of that cash. Nemeth said cash generation through the cycle also enables investment in organic initiatives and strategic mergers and acquisitions, which Patrick expects to remain a priority.
The latest results provide context for those competing demands. Third-quarter net sales were $975 million, compared with $976 million a year earlier, while operating income declined to $50 million from $66 million. For the first nine months of 2026, operating cash flow was $147 million, down from $199 million in the prior-year period. Patrick attributed the change to working-capital deployment supporting its composite-products growth strategy and inventory management for customers.
Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow, which Patrick defines as operating cash flow less purchases of property, plant and equipment, was $203 million through the third quarter, compared with $211 million a year earlier. At quarter-end, Patrick had approximately $716 million of available liquidity, comprising borrowing availability under its credit facility and cash on hand, alongside about $1.4 billion of total debt and a total net leverage ratio of 2.9x under its credit agreement.
The immediate capital return is therefore the scheduled December dividend. The replenished authorization establishes capacity for future repurchases rather than current activity, with its use constrained by the merger restrictions while Patrick continues to fund operations, organic initiatives and acquisitions.
